hook_text: In 1885, thousands of miners moved behind a fence they could not leave for months.
clip_script: Kimberley, the 1870s. Young men walk for weeks from Pedi country, Lesotho and Mozambique to dig for diamonds. They earn money for guns, cattle and ploughs, then walk home. But the mine owners want workers who stay and accept low pay. 1872: pass laws. No pass, no freedom to move. 1885: the closed compounds. Barracks behind high fences, wire mesh overhead. Workers stay inside for three to six months, searched every day, buying food from the company shop. The companies say it stops diamond theft. It also stops workers leaving or asking for more pay. And only black workers are locked in. This system will be copied on the gold mines and shape South Africa for a century.
visual_style: A whiteboard map with walking routes converging on Kimberley, then a pass document stamped, then a compound drawn as a rectangle of barracks with a fence and mesh roof closing over it.
pacing: Steady build, slowing when the fence closes.
